title: Be strong (Joshua 1:1–9)
hookLine: Moses' successor is told three times, "be strong and of good courage"
last: THE STORY GOES ON WITHOUT MOSES.

cards: What do you say to someone on the first morning of a job far too big for them? Joshua has just stepped into Moses' place. The book's first verse calls him Moses' minister, his assistant.
Now there's a river in front of him, a land of walled cities beyond it, and a whole people watching to see what happens next. God speaks.
There's a promise of the land, border to border, but no battle plan, no tactics, no word about the walls. There's one phrase, said, then said again, then a third time.
And before the chapter ends, someone says it back to him.

teach.b: Listen for the repeat. First: be strong and of good courage, because you will lead this people into the land. That one is for the task.
Then again, stronger: only be strong and very courageous. And the reason is a surprise. Not to fight.

teach.h: SECOND: FOR THE TEACHING, DAY AND NIGHT.
teach.b: To keep the teaching Moses gave, turning from it neither to the right nor to the left. Then the line: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night."
The bravest thing asked of the new leader isn't a battle. It's to keep studying, to keep the words in his mouth.

Then a third time, with a third reason: be strong and of good courage, don't be afraid, don't be dismayed, "for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The work, the teaching, and company.
Now skip to the end of the chapter. Joshua gives his first orders, and the tribes whose land lies east of the Jordan answer him. Whatever you command, we'll do.
Wherever you send us, we'll go. And they close with the very words he was given: only be strong and of good courage.
The encouragement that came down to Joshua goes back up to him from the people. So courage here isn't a mood you wait for. It's a command.
It can be spoken, repeated and handed on, from God to a leader, and from a crowd to the person in front of it.

how: The words chazak ve'ematz, be strong and of good courage, come from Joshua 1, and some say the phrase to encourage someone taking on a new task.

o: a battle cry shouted as the walls fell
chazak: the charge given to Joshua three times
a vow the tribes swore to Moses at his death

games.q: be strong, three times — tap the pairs.
p: you will lead the people into the land
to keep the teaching, day and night
God is with you wherever you go

s: God tells Joshua to be strong only for the battles ahead
the second time, the reason is the teaching: meditate therein day and night.
the people say be strong back to Joshua
at the end of chapter one the tribes answer: only be strong and of good courage.
Joshua is given a battle plan in chapter one
no tactics: a promise of the land, a book to keep in his mouth, and be strong.

games.q: you're one of the tribes. Joshua, the new leader, has just given his first orders. how do you answer him?
o: wait and see if he's as good as Moses.
promise to follow, and tell him to be strong.
ask for Moses' plans in writing first.
games.why: they promise to go wherever he sends them, and end with the words he was just given: only be strong and of good courage.

practice: Name, quietly, one thing this week that feels too big.
Then say be strong, aloud or under your breath, three times: once for the task, once for what you're trying to stay faithful to while you do it, once for the people who are in it with you.
If you pray, add the verse's last words: the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.

wordCard.voice: Be strong. Chazak, in Hebrew, said to Joshua three times, and then said back to him by the people. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: be strong and of good courage, the phrase of Joshua 1.

carryVoice: Your line: be strong, again. Courage can be handed on, and handed back. See you tomorrow.
